speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FRANGOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, as a private member of this honourable house I rise to a question of privilege. By virtue of section 133 of the British North America Act and of numerous orders in council, particularly P. C. 159 of January 31, 1928, members of parliament are entitled to an English and French copy of all official publications. I hold in my hand administrator's order, A-317, issued by Mr. A. H. Williamson, administrator of supplies, on July 30, 1942, approved by Mr. D. Gordon, chairman, wartime prices and trade board and concurred in by Mr. R. C. Berkinshaw, chairman, wartime industries control board. I am credibly informed that this document has never been translated into French because of orders that were issued not to translate it.
For some time I have been receiving copies of another publication issued by Mr. John Grierson entitled " Nouvelles Catholiques." This comes from the wartime information board, and I am informed that it has never been translated into English. I believe that some issues are made up largely of translations of material appearing in English publications, but the English text has not been sent to us. I exercise my right as a member of the House of Commons to ask for a French 
translation of order A-317 and an English translation or the English text, as the case may be, of all numbers of " Nouvelles Catholiques." I protest strongly against the propaganda contained in order A-317 for the English speaking population exclusively, and against the issuing of "Nouvelles Catholiques" for the French speaking population exclusively. One is for the English and the other is for the French, and they are contradictory.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
Last evening I was dealing with a few instances of expenditures under the wartime information board. To-day I intend, after making reference to a few further instances, to deal generally with the question of information and publicity, coming as it does within the terms of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) and seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), wherein it is proposed that a recommendation be made

. . . that said committee have power to investigate expenditures incurred for publicity or in relation thereto by wartime information board and by various governmental departments and boards, subsequent to March 31, 1942.
I wonder whether I could get some order-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
-in accordance with the courtesy I always extend to other hon. members.
I was dealing with certain salaries paid to members of the wartime information board.
I refer now to Mr. McKenna, in charge of external news distribution, receiving a salary of $5,200 a year, and to Mr. L. L. Knott, receiving $4,800 and certain expenses-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: Order. There is loud conversation through the whole of the chamber. I would ask for silence so that I can follow the hon. member.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker;-and expenses amounting to $633.25. Another official, the chief of the research section, receives a salary of $6,000 a year and
travelling expenses. There is another executive officer, whose duties relate to publicity matters as they affect French Canada, who receives $5,000 a year, with $782 expenses. Another official, Mr. Andrew, in charge of the media analysis section, receives a salary of $4,500 a year.
The situation is this, that in the first year of the war the former war information board, the bureau of public information, expended $202.672; whereas this new body has expended, during a period of a little over six and a half months, the sum of $579,000.
One would think, having regard to the tremendous increase of expenditure on publicity under this board, there would not be expenditures for publicity in other departments of government. What do we find? Practically every department has its own publicity liaison officers or press agents. According to sessional paper 216, the reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), "How many press agents or liaison officers are there in the employ of the government or any commission or other authority connected, therewith under each separate minister?" a situation is revealed which in my opinion is totally unjustifiable. The only way in which it can be investigated and the proper savings effected is through submission of the accounts and the whole matter of publicity to the public accounts committee.
In so far as the Department of Finance is concerned the reply given is that there are three such officials, receiving respectively $5,000-together with actual out-of-pocket living and travelling expenses-$3,600 and $2,600 a year. The Department of Labour has a director of information responsible for the preparation of press material and public information, and who receives $4,500. The Department of Munitions and Supply states that it has no officers whose work is solely liaison, but it names a number of officials who are charged with the preparation of press announcements, of material for radio and screen, compiling, writing and so on, and the number of these is nine. The Department of National Defence has forty-eight persons employed on publicity work, five of whom are civilians and forty-three officers. The five civilians receive salaries of from $3,500 to $6,000 per year. The Department of National Defence for Air has forty-one such officers and officials, of whom six are civilians; one of them, Mr. Clark, receiving $6,500 and actual out-of-pocket expenses while absent from Ottawa; another, Mr. Brown, receiving $5,830 and actual living expenses; another receiving $5,800 per annum; another $4,000; and there are two with salaries of
Public Accounts

$3,500. Then there is the Department of National Defence, with one director and nine liaison officers. The film commissioner has three production liaison officers receiving salaries from $280 per month to $325 per month. The wartime prices and trade board has nineteen press agents.
What does all this mean? It means that during the past few months not only have publicity costs in Canada increased by hundreds of thousands of dollars, but in addition to that there are press agents in all the departments I have mentioned-and I do not think I have covered them all-whose purpose is to assist the press in giving out information to the people of Canada. Having regard to the numbers of these officials, and that many of them must be engaged in the duplication of work, and the obvious possibility of reducing their numbers very greatly if there were any investigation, I submit that there is a sufficient excuse for the submission of this matter to the public accounts committee.
We have arrived at the position in Canada where information is controlled by the government, as it must be during a time of war by censorship regulations, so as to prevent information going out which would be of benefit to the enemy. But there is further control than that. We are controlled to-day until quite often, in the reports that go out, the prime qualification seems to be adulation of the government and everlasting praise of the ministers of the crown. From these departments emanate regularly articles and propaganda, and in my opinion they can be justified only on the ground that praise of the government is to be disseminated. I suggest that if there were a proper investigation of this matter we could save, if not hundreds of thousands of dollars, at any rate a very substantial amount of money. A substantial reduction could take place in every department and the result would certainly be no detriment to the government while on the other hand it would be of great benefit to Canada's war effort.
The wartime information board and the other departments connected with publicity should have as their aim and purpose the enlightenment of the Canadian people on the progress of the war, and the desire to arouse determination among Canadians throughout the country, to kindle and to continue to rekindle the fires of patriotism.
I examine the pamphlets that come out from time to time from the various departments and hear some of the broadcasts that are made, and I wonder sometimes if the object is not to use publicity in Canada to-day as a vehicle for the government's own

personal purposes. My hon. friends on the government side will not agree with that. Go from one end of Canada to the other, however, and listen to the conversations that take place; if there is one criticism against the government it is that too often the publicity that is being disseminated is party propaganda.
I ask, what defence has ever been given by any minister of the crown to the allegations that are common in practically the entire press of Canada, that too great expenditures were being made by the wartime information board? It comes under the Prime Minister's department, and he has never offered any defence nor made any justification of the ampunt allowed and the tremendous salaries paid. No minister of the crown has ever defended them. No minister of the crown yesterday defended the expenditures that were being made. The only defence that has been offered at all was the defence by Mr. Grierson, the general manager, in a letter written to the press, in which he said that the salaries that were being paid were in the main defensible, and that there had been a few out-of-line salary expenses but that these had been adjusted. Those who should defend such over-expenditures as are revealed not only in the wartime information board but for publicity in other departments of government as well, should be brought before a committee of parliament and not be given an opportunity of providing thereto only an ex parte defence through the medium of the press of Canada.
I will read what Mr. Grierson said in the article in question. He pointed out that he had not been in the position long, and I am not criticizing him at the moment. What I do know is that these salaries are out of line, and one would have expected the Minister of Finance to be the fir$t to raise strenuous objections to such salaries being paid in war time.

find out before the public accounts committee. We want to know just why these salaries are being paid and what justification there is for the multiplication of officials in these various publicity branches in the past few months. I was about to quote Mr. Grierson:
Information will be blamed for not solving the division between some people in Quebec and some people elsewhere. ... It will be blamed, for not bridging divisions which are sometimes geographical, racial and religious, but often political.
I suggest that it is the duty of the wartime information board to arouse the people of Canada. That is its responsibility just as it is the responsibility that rests upon all of us. How do pamphlets such as I have in my hand at the moment, issued by the information branch, entitled "Nouvelles Catholiques", in any way contribute to the war effort of the dominion? How can they in any way be considered as proper matters for distribution by the war information board? To whom shall this whole matter be submitted?
The leader of the government, yesterday, when he advocated submission of this matter to the war expenditures committee, in answer to the following pertinent question by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) at page 2816-
Will the minister undertake that if the investigation of matters connected with the operation of the wartime information board is referred to the war expenditures committee, such investigation will be in open and not in secret meetings?
Replied as follows:-
No, I can say at once to my hon. friend that I will' give no such undertaking.
And a little later on

and I wish to be fair-he said this:
And you will find out, in the proper way. But there may be expenditures in connection with the operation of the wartime information board, as there would be in connection with the operation of the defence board, which it would not be in the public interest to divulge at the present time.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether or not the examination of the expenditures in connection with the administration of the board can, by any stretch of the imagination, be considered as not in the public interest. "Not in the public interest", has been a term, a vehicle, a medium, dragged into this chamber on so many occasions, and used as a method through which information to which the public is entitled has been denied.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: That was established in the mother of parliaments, as a basic .parliamentary practice.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
True, as the minister has said, "in the public interest", when utilized in the mother of parliaments as an answer to a question asked, invariably suggests and demands the respect of those who receive the answer. They realize that it is not in the public interest. But to ask what justification there may be for these expenditures, and to inquire what savings could be effected, and what expenditures for publicity could be reduced after careful examination, cannot by any stretch of the imagination come within the purview of the defence that it is not in the public interest.
Again I ask the minister: Why deny members of parliament the right to examine these accounts? Why deny them the right which has been theirs for hundreds of years, namely the right to examine expenditures, the right to ask that they be scrutinized? We are offered the right to have these matters submitted to a committee not yet set up, and in any event, to a committee behind closed doors. We should have the right held by members of the British House of Commons, of having investigations in the open, where publicity has the effect of preventing those of like mind from carrying on in a similar fashion. I appeal to the acting leader of the government to-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: Does the hon. member want an answer to the question he has asked?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
The minister may answer later. I appeal to him to give to members of the house their right to have full information and the right to make examination of these expenditures. I demand it in the name of the people of Canada from one end of the country to the other who to-day are saying to us that we are not asserting our rights in failing to demand careful scrutiny of all expenditures.
Only yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that the responsibility for the setting up of the public accounts committee rested upon the opposition.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: I did not say that at all. I said nothing about setting up the committee. The government sets up the committee. I referred to the calling together of the committee.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
The minister said the responsibility rested upon the opposition. Only the other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) gave a similar lecture to the opposition in regard to another matter. To-day, so that there will be no doubt about the question, on behalf of this official opposition, and speaking with the knowledge and consent of all members in it, I demand the right to which we are entitled-the right of examination, the right to assure the people of
Public Accounts

Canada that every dollar spent shall be fairly and properly spent. We may be told that the public accounts committee, as at present constituted, has not the power to examine into these accounts. Parliament can give it that power. All we are asking is that parliament do give to the committee the right to investigate expenditures which, in amount, have been shocking to many people throughout the dominion.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intend to follow rather closely the arguments which have been advanced by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who has just taken his seat. But before doing so there is a general question which came to my mind when this barrage or attack opened yesterday afternoon. I ask the question on the floor of the house. All hon. members know that the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is the one responsible for the wartime information board. We all know the Prime Minister is absent in Washington on very important duties, and I just wonder why the Tory strategists should choose this as the opportune time to launch a bitter and vicious attack upon the expenditures of the wartime information board.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext:
Oh, just be patient. My memory went back to some months ago when, in the British House of Commons during the absence of Mr. Churchill, a dastardly attempt was made to stab him in the back. I remember too the welL-deserved rebuke the British House of Commons gave to that performance. And, Mr. Speaker, I prophesy the present performance will suffer the same deserved fate. I cannot, within the rules of this house, state that this is a deliberate attempt to stab the Prime Minister in the back; but I can say this, that I do not believe in Santa Claus, nor do I believe in coincidence. And before I forget, it will be recalled that yesterday the genial leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) offered gratuitously a great amount of advice to the government. May I tender a bit of advice to him, and it is this: I suggest that if he wishes to raise the esteem of the Progressive Conservative party in the minds of the Canadian people he should fire its present board of pin-pricking strategists and appoint a board of strategy whose sole and only purpose will be an honest-to-God effort to win this var.
Obviously the present amendment was purposely timed because it has nothing to do with the motion. The motion was only

the routine motion to permit the committee to have its proceedings printed, and to sit while the house is sitting. Then comes a substantive motion in the form of an amendment-and while the Prime Minister is absent. I do not think much of that kind of courage. In addition, for the benefit of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), w1k>
occasionally has much to say, I will add this: I do not think much of the personal courage-of a member who by innuendo and indirect methods attempts to undermine confidence in any war board at this time. We have not had one specific charge from one member of the opposition that John Doe is not fit for his job or is not doing his job well. We have not had one specific instance of waste. All we have had is a blanket charge that over half a million dollars is being spent in publicizing Canada's war effort and that therefore there must be waste and reckless expenditure of public money. Not one hon. member has had the personal courage to tell this house of one single specific item of waste.
Now I come to the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). In his opening remarks, with the very solemn air that distinguishes him, he shook his head and in funereal and pontifical tones stated:
I suggest that this debate has illustrated a point which we in the opposition have been endeavouring to make for a very considerable time.
Then he shook his finger at me. And he went on:
It is that ive, the members of parliament, are denied the opportunity of looking into expenditures, and we are denied it time and again.
My answer to that is not by way of inference or innuendo. I say to the hon. member that in time of war, lip service and lip loyalty are not good enough. I am going to quote to this house from the official record to show the attendance of the Conservative members of the war expenditures committee, these gentlemen who to-day rise in their places and say they are denied the right to check public expenditures. I ask that they be judged by their performance, not by their lip service. I hold in my hand the official record obtained from the clerk of the war expenditures committee, of which both the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member who moved this amendment were members.

It is generally ready to spend thousands of dollars yearly in publicizing its products in order to sell them. The Wrigley chewing gum company spends thousands of dollars annually on sales campaigns. whether the money being spent to publicize the Conservative party during a time of war is money that should be going into the coffers of this government as excess profits to help to win the war?
As I view the matter it settles down to a simple problem. Accusations of waste of public money by the wartime information board have been made. So far as I am concerned, and I think every member of the committee will agree with me, even my hon. friends of the opposition, I contend that since the accusation has been made, the matter should be thoroughly investigated and thoroughly sifted. If there is any extravagance, it should be stopped. The whole issue is whether this problem should be referred to the war expenditures committee or to the public accounts committee.
The argument has been advanced by the hon. member for Lake Centre that the matter should not be referred to the war expenditures committee, and: he gives two reasons which I should like to discuss. In the first place, he says that the meetings of the war expenditures committee are held in camera, whereas the meetings of the public accounts committee are held in public; therefore he believes that the matter should be investigated by the public accounts committee. The reason for this sharp divergence in viewpoint, is a simple one. It all depends on the results that you seek to achieve. If you wish a businesslike investigation along the lines of British practice; if you wish a committee that will sit down and seriously study the problem, search out any extravagance that is going on and curb it; if you wish a committee that will reach a unanimous conclusion, a committee that will do all this work without giving political kudos to anyone, then refer the matter to the war expenditures committee. It may be said that I am prejudiced because I am on the war expenditures committee, but I should like to remind the house of the manner in which this committee functions.
As one illustration I shall quote from one of our reports. When we investigated the operations of the British Commonwealth air training plan in 1941 we checked the efficiency and cost of operating the elementary flying training schools and the air observer schools. The meetings were held in camera, and I have no right to refer to any evidence that was given, but I have the fullest possible right to read from the report of the committee. The short extract from the report which I shall read will indicate clearly to the house the basis upon which the war expenditures committee faces

any problem in regard to the waste of public money. I am reading from a report dated November 3, 1941, later tabled in the house, as follows:
The subcommitte has carefully considered the question of profits which will be earned by the operating companies.
This refers to the air observer schools.
Partly on account of highly efficient management and partly on account of the pupil intake as fixed by the contract being increased without proportionate increase in management costs it was found that substantial profits were being earned.
What did the committee do? Did they blazon across Canada in the press of this country that the air observer schools and the elementary flying training schools were being operated at a profit three or four times greater than they should receive? Of course we did not do that. What would that have done to the morale of the staffs of these schools which were doing such a wonderful job? We approached the problem in a businesslike manner.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT
speechtext: Was it a fact that they were operating at a cost three or four times greater than they should have been?

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT

I am coming to that. The report continues:
The subcommittee fully appreciates the fact that the air observer schools are being very efficiently managed and that these schools are performing an important war task and also appreciates the fact that measures of economy should not be permitted to slow up our war effort but as the actual circumstances have altered sharply since the contract was first entered into the subcommittee decided that a conference should be called of executive officers representing all of the schools, that the facts should be frankly placed before them and their cooperation invited. The conference was held on June 4 and as a result the operating companies have all voluntarily offered to agree to a reduction of what is described in the agreement as flying hour profits from $1 per flying hour to 35 cents per flying hour.
That was a reduction of approximately sixty-five per cent in the profits of the air observer schools. That was done without any publicity, without any detrimental effect upon the operation of the schools. It was done immediately, and in part the reduction was made voluntarily on a retroactive basis. That is the way the war expenditures committee functions, and that is the way I submit that it should function. It is not our job to do any mud slinging; it is not our job to slow up the war effort, but it is our job to search out any waste and to see that it is cured and cured as quickly as possible.

Expenditures of five or six billion dollars have been made, and to date the war expenditures committee has not investigated an amount in excess of ten million dollars.
I was positively shocked when I heard that statement. I could not believe my ears. From the inception of the committee I have been chairman of subcommittee No. 1 and I know something of the work of that committee. To make a statement that the whole committee in its two years of service has checked less than ten million dollars of expenditures is simply shocking. I should like to give a short account of what one subcommittee, one-third of the whole committee, has done.
This very last year, 1942, we carefully checked the aircraft programme in this country, a programme running into over 81,000 million. We called into the committee every contract for the production of aeroplanes that has been given in Canada since the outbreak of war. These contracts, totalling over SI,000 million, were divided among the members of the committee, who studied them carefully and reported individually on each contract to the committee. We were not content with that. We called in the director of aircraft production and the solicitors who helped to negotiate these contracts, also five accountants representing the three hundred odd accountants who are constantly busy in the Department of Munitions and Supply auditing, cost accounting and the like, and on top of that, Mr. Speaker, your subcommittee visited every plant manufacturing aeroplanes in Canada, except one. At the time of our visit we took evidence from the executive officers, the manager and secretary-treasurer of these plants. That whole production programme was carefully checked, and notwithstanding the fact that we had two Conservative members on the committee and one Social Credit member, all of whom made a real contribution to the work of the committee, we brought in a unanimous report.
In addition to that, we checked the work of wartime housing, -which at the time of our check ran into an expenditure of over forty million dollars, and we brought in a unanimous report on that.

I have already outlined the other steps we took. I will also say this, and I challenge any member of the subcommittee to contradict it. The fullest possible information was obtained on every occasion. Every member of the committee was given the fullest latitude in asking questions. No information was denied us. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of this house, that we made the best check that we could of the different subjects that were referred to us, and we brought in a unanimous report. If there was anj'thing wrong with 
our report, why did not the Conservative members dissent and bring in a minority report? They did not dissent, because they agreed with everything that we did.
I suggest to you. sir, that the members of the house who now want to refer the checking of the expenditure of the wartime information board to the public accounts committee are not very much interested in economy. I do not think they are interested in anything but political advantage, and mighty temporary advantage at that.
For the reasons I have outlined, I intend to Vote against the amendment, and I would urge every member of the house to think seriously before he would send this matter to the public accounts committee in view of the record of the public accounts committee in the past. Just where did you get with your Bren gun inquiry? Just where did you get with the Thompson rug inquiry? Does it help Canada's war effort to put on a bear-garden performance? We should like to inquire why it has not been translated into French. We should also like to inquire from the board whether this order A-317 has not been given the same publicity as the others because it induces people to commit crimes-and I mean what I say.

1. For the purposes of this order,
(d)	"primary importer" shall mean the importer or wholesaler who first takes delivery in Canada of any shipment of condoms imported from outside Canada;
(e)	"wholesaler" shall mean any person who buys, deals in, sells and distributes condoms to any retailer and who does not, in the ordinary course of business, sell such goods at retail;

Nothing in this order shall be construed as prohibiting:

(b)	a wholesaler from continuing to sell any condoms which he had in stock as at the date hereof.
(e) a retailer from continuing to sell any condoms which he had in stock as at the date hereof.
This word is known everywhere, and it has been defined as "a contraceptive shield." I have here a book written by Doctor Ryberg, of Toronto, and at page 112 he states:
The condom is not only for protection against disease, but as a precaution against pregnancy.
And, at page 155:
The condom. The word "contraceptive" may be applied to any preparation or appliance that can be used by either the man or the woman to prevent conception. The appliance perhaps most in use throughout the world is the "condom".
Finally. Mr. Speaker, I would refer to the criminal code, section 207:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who knowingly, without lawful justification or excuse, . . .
(c)	offers to sell, advertises, publishes an advertisement of, or has for sale or disposal any means or instructions or any medicine, drug or article intended or represented as a means of preventing conception. . . .
That is a provision of the criminal code. This is why it would be important to know from the wartime information board if instructions have been given by somebody to hide this order No. A-317, because it is altogether contrary to the provisions of the criminal code.
Mr. .T. L. CHURCH (Broadview): In rising to take part in the debate on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), I wish to express my entire disagreement with what has just been said by the hon. member for Hal ton (Mr. Cleaver) regarding those who sit on this side of the house. Since the war started I have never known of any "politicians" in our group; we are trying to help the government so long as they conduct a total war effort.
I have known the hon. member for Halton a long time. I knew his father. I remember the hon. member as a young lawyer who practised after the war, I believe in Burlington. I think he was a reeve, and afterwards became mayor, in 1920. At the time, we were negotiating the so-called Hamilton highway from Toronto to Hamilton, and our city gave forty per cent of the money towards it. The hon. member represents a traditionally Conservative seat. I have had a great deal to do with the county council and municipalities of the county of Halton in connection with removing franchises affecting light, power and transportation, in Ontario as head of the municipalities, and so securing the people of that county some relief. It was a Conservative administration which gave his riding the privileges they enjoy to-day in regard to light, power and transportation.
The more I reflect on the question before the house, the more I am convinced that this whole problem of publicity and the wartime information bureau should not go to the public accounts committee at all. A royal commission should be appointed to investigate the waste of money which has gone on since the war began in respect of publicity and information bureaus.
The hon. member for Halton, in attacking those on this side, said that he has heard a Conservative publicity man is being paid $10,000 a year, and he asks, who is paying him? I ask him, if that is so, why does he not tell the house and the country who is paying him? Why not do something along those lines? Why does he not say something about the funds collected in connection with the Beauharnois scandal? I fought this deal for many years in the house, and, very largely owing to my opposition-at the start, alone-they later got me out of the house for two or three years.
I have opposed, consistently since this war started, the creation of boards such as this. The board is an utter waste of money. It is duplicating work which is being done by the press and radio of this country. In England the same trouble arose since the war in connection with the information bureau and the British broadcasting corporation. Complaints first arose when hundreds of thousands of pounds sterling were spent in dropping leaflets over Germany. Then the BBC had Mr. Peterson, who had said a few months before
Public Accounts

the war broke out that anyone who proposed rearmament should be committed to gaol for life and given bread and water. That is the kind of thing which was doled out to the British people, with the result that Britain threw away her defences and her friends and faced not only insult and invasion but almost extinction as a nation.
The amendment proposes to recommit the report to the public accounts committee and enable them to go into all moneys spent on publicity, not only by the board but by various government departments, including the military service departments. I have no quarrel with hon. gentlemen opposite; far from it. Many of them are among the best men who have attained public experience in municipal work, and came here from that fine service. My old friend the chairman of the standing orders committee was a splendid head of a municipality. The young member for Halton has come up along the same road. I am very much surprised at his remarks, because he must know that an acid test of dictatorship is the policy of muzzling the press by force and controlling the sources of information. The press is in a double sense, as I said before, an intermediary between the government and the people. It provides a channel by which ministers can keep the electors informed of their activities, and it also serves as a kind of barometer by which the government can gauge the feeling of the country. A press, subject to official pressure will give a wholly false impression of public opinion. The correspondence columns of a great newspaper reflect public opinion, or should do so; they should not refuse to publish letters which may be contrary to the editorial policy of the paper. Without a free press, dictatorships usurp power and we see the results in the axis countries to-day.
I might point out to the hon. member for Halton that his and many other county councils are complaining about the extravagance of governments, dominion, provincial and municipal. I have talked with some of the municipal authorities of that fine county, and I can tell you that the people of that county and others in Ontario are complaining about the action of parliament in these matters.
What is the public accounts committee for? Are only the majority to obtain a hearing? Where do the minority come in? The two old parties are on trial at the bar of public opinion; so indeed are hon. gentlemen to the left and every member of this house. The public hold us responsible when we hand over control to boards of all kinds which spend money like water. Much money has been spent.with no effort to stop it. The auditor general's hands are tied behind his back,

although he is an officer of parliament. Then another official, the comptroller of the treasury, is appointed, and likewise his hands are tied behind his back; these men can do nothing, they are just officials of the treasury department. People are beginning to lose confidence in us as members and in the way we do business here because we allow such conditions as this, permitting our rights and powers and privileges to be taken from us and handed over to public bodies which can raise the prices of coal and food and everything else, though not one dollar of their expenses can be accounted for to this house, which is supposed to vote and control the money.
The issue before the public accounts committee to-day is, are we getting value for our money, or are we spending money like water, much of it not for the war effort. What check have we over expenditures? If any municipal council spent money as we do it would go bankrupt in no time. The municipal governments have auditors to check every dollar that is spent. They are required by law to have such a check on expenditures. Moreover, the treasurer is sworn and so is the mayor. They are sworn to conduct the business of the municipality in a proper manner and to see that the people get value for the money they pay in taxation. I remember visiting the county of Halton at the time the people in that municipality voted on public ownership bylaws for light, power and transportation, and were relieved from the powers that be. The privately-owned utilities authorities had a strangle-hold on them and they got free.
I object to the information that is given by the wartime information board. We have got into an unseemly wrangle over this whole question, which could have been avoided if the government had gone about the matter in a sensible way and decided to refer it all to the public accounts committee. In England they have reduced their estimates for the work of disseminating information. There is a pile of literature two feet high in Canada collected by the wartime information board and it is distributed to the newspaper offices. It goes to the editorial rooms of the rural papers, and the irony of it is that some rural editors are being put out of business. The small newspaper man to-day has not a chance. The rural newspapers in former days represented the great body of wise, independent thought in the country, but they have been practically put out of business by government agencies. There are some excellent old, reputable newspapers, Liberal, . Conservative, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, Social Credit, which have been driven to the wall by controls, so that a man

Public Accounts
cannot, from the commercial aspect, conduct an honest newspaper in an honest way for the good of the people. These newspapers have suffered in two wars and a long depression with increased costs, from the reflection cast upon them by the government through the appointment of an information bureau to fulfil the function that has been that of the newspaper from time immemorial.
I object to these expenditures. I fancy that most of the information that comes from the board goes into the waste-paper basket which is the most useful piece of furniture in any office I know of for a great deal of literature published by the board. I do not wish to reflect in any way upon the committee, because I have a great many friends on that committee, good members of parliament. They do the best they can, but I am bound to say that I found it necessary to resign because I did not believe that it would do the work for which it was intended. I was a member of the committee and I resigned.
Years ago I played my part in protecting an investment of $100,000,000 of public funds spent by the city of Toronto in connection with a great project there in light, power and transportation, and I can assure you that those of us who were charged with safeguarding the public at that time insisted upon a perfect audit and safeguard of all the moneys that were spent. It could not be shown that one dollar had been misspent, and we had inquiries conducted into the development of the harbour and other utilities in order to make sure that no money would be wasted and not a dollar misspent in an honest administration. The same is true of the work that was done in connection with the development of light, power and transportation facilities. I suggest that if we adopted the same principle here that the municipalities have it would bring satisfactory results.
Yesterday the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) made a reference to me. He mentioned something about the coalscuttle and suggested that I had brought up that question. I simply mentioned it to show that the farmers wanted value from their government for the money they paid in taxes. The coal-scuttle is also a useful thing. I know it has been useful to me as a receptacle for much of the information that comes from this board. The Minister of Pensions and National Health might also find it serviceable for some of the information that has been going around, such as, for instance, .the rumour that was heard about everyone paying 50 cents each for social
security and receiving in return food, clothing, everything that was needed, and at least one bottle of medicine for the week-end.
Take some of the information that this board hands out. About a week after the Dieppe raid we saw a long white sheet of paper from the bureau with a heading something like this, "The Yanks did it." That is a name that I would not use with reference to our great ally, but the information bureau used it. But the point is that the information the bureau gave was wrong, because Mr. Churchill made a statement in the British House of Commons on September 8 and again on September 11, on Armistice day, in which he showed what Canada had done, and who was responsible for the raid. So that the information given by the bureau did not represent the facts; it was false. I am sorry I have not the pamphlet here; if I had I would quote it.
There is another institution known to-day as the Gallup poll. It is all gallop and no poll. No one is taking any poll. In fact, the polls are all Liberal newspapers or government agencies within newspaper offices. I have a great deal of respect for a good Liberal and I have voted for some in municipal elections. I know many fine people who are Liberals. I believe, however, that they take their politics too seriously, especially in the public accounts committee. My hon. friend, the member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), made a good speech, but I may say that his father, whom I knew for a long time, had, when I knew him, a different view of these questions. I think it would be a good thing if the two main parties would revise these heavy public expenditures and protect the treasury. There are some wise public policies I believe in, namely, always tell the people the truth. Never be afraid of telling the public that you have made a mistake. The people do not expect their leaders to be gods. Trust the people and they will trust you, and never legislate against human nature.
In my opinion this debate will do a lot of good. None of us want to hang around here much longer, and. personally I should like to see the house close up in another month. It would certainly be a godsend to most of us because I think that most of us want to get away from this place, seeing that we have no power left with war being blamed for all these controls. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said yesterday, and I agree with him, that we might as well put a padlock on the door of the House of Commons for all the good we can do, with all our rights and privileges denied us.

I have never read anything to compare with this return that has been brought down here, sessional paper 176, on this information bureau. Just think of it: 84,500 to a housemaster! I do not know of any school that could afford to pay him that salary. The principal of a large high school, with two or three thousand pupils under his supervision, would not get that sum. The main objection to this institution is that the publicity bureau does not give correct information and it duplicates the better done work of newspapers. The Gallup poll started about the same time as they did, but I do not know of any cabinet minister or any member of parliament who has a vote. I am glad to see the acting Prime Minister looking so well; I do not know whether he has a vote on the Gallup poll or not, or if he is on the voters' list. If he has it must keep him galloping around the [DOT] country to record his vote. The truth is that it is very largely a newspaper or information board or government invention, and most of those who take part in it have some affiliation with some newspapers supporting the government. The poll is under no government regulation.
Then there is the censorship board. I suggest that the sooner this useless censorship board' is abolished the better for everyone. Many of its employees are running to the newspaper offices and whenever anything is criticized here they try to prevent any word of it getting into the newspapers. Personally, I do not mind saying that I am past the stage of this game where it matters to me whether my name appears in the newspapers or not. It makes no difference whatever to me whether I am reported in the newspapers or not so long as I know that I have done my duty. When Mr. Churchill, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, speaks, he tells the people the plain truth; he does not mince his words and the people listen to him and trust him.
The other day Mr. Bracken announced that there would be a considerable reduction in the estimates of the British information bureau for this year. I might refer to a saying of Lord Salisbury in this connection. He said once of his colleague, the Duke of Devonshire, that, to show his impartiality, he could talk one way and vote another. That is what we have seen in the last session or two. Those who opposed the plebiscite rose in their places and voted for it.
Then we have these so-called information bureaus. They are established, and a lot of what they do is wrong. A good many have been sent to New York. Reference was made yesterday to Mr. Casey, or "Casey at the bat,"

who has now gone to parts unknown. I understand he has become the head of Republican publicity for a political party, but at one time he was on the payroll here at a salary of $13,320, with $2,836 living allowance and S800 travelling expenses. Another gentleman was Mr. Lash of the Canadian National Railways. I should say that gentleman has done more for disunity in Canada during the past two years than anyone else I know, since the figures he issued from the information bureau with respect to enlistments in military districts were proved to be wrong.
Then, there is another gentleman, a great favourite of the publicity bureau. I do not know why he was even sent out to Canada, but the information bureau, or that part of it having to do with publicity, has been issuing his speeches and paying for them out of public funds. This is the gentleman who was asked to take the salute the other day in England by two or three brigades, composed of men. some of whom came from Toronto, the city I represent, and from other parts of Canada. This gentleman is being boomed by the bureau, and more or less by the government in Canada, for what I do not know. I would say that what the information bureau should have said about him is that recently Mr. Malcolm MacDonald, Britain's trade commissioner, whom this bureau supports, has been going around the United States and Canada, and making speeches in England about Canada. He has been taking salutes. This is the same gentleman who, after the war broke out-possibly a year after-went to see Lord Craigavon, the Prime Minister of Ulster, and said over there that he was quite willing to make military arrangements. Lord Craigavon was willing to make those arrangements, but Mr. de Valera would not agree to back Ulster up, so that Eire left Ulster in the British empire to fight alone, and Eire became neutral. Malcolm MacDonald went to Ireland and put pressure upon Ulster to agree to some such neutrality arrangement. When we think of the facts of the case, it is monstrous that a British cabinet minister and British newspapers could be found to urge this course on Ulster, when the mother country was being bombed'-

So far as this country is concerned we have our own newspaper representatives going to the United States. I understood no references to race or religion were to. be made in parliament. I never have made them. And yet I find one document issued by the publicity bureau, in one language, and put out free by the wartime information board, from its distribution branch in Ottawa, April 24, 1943, a religious publication of only one religion. I know nothing about any similar pamphlets put out at government expense by the Baptist church, the Presbyterian church, the United church, or the Anglican church, or any other church; but certainly one particular church alone seems to be favoured
by this board. I believe if money is to be spent on church news, all should be given equal treatment.
One of the Canadian editors sent by the bureau went to the United States and at Washington, in lauding the war effort of that country, made the statement over the United States radio and was reported in the press to the effect that the improvement in Anglo-American relations could be attributed in part to the victories in North Africa by General Montgomery's eighth army. He said, in part:
I think Americans, and Canadians to a lesser extent, were prone to believe that British generals were a lot of brass hats and that the British Tommy had lost his fighting spirit.
What kind of information is that to give to the people in the United States at this time, and particularly when it is all wrong? Seventy-six per cent of General Montgomery's eighth army that marched 1,600 miles across Africa came from the British isles. Ninety per cent of General Alexander's army came from the British isles, and the other ten per cent from the dominions, particularly New Zealand, Australia, India and South Africa. So that it is not I who needs to be mor.e careful, but rather the people on the board. I never state anything but facts I believe to be true. I know all I have said to-day is true. I have the information to back up what I say.
Then, there are departmental bureaus, some of which have been travelling to Los Angeles and Great Britain. The Canadian people are assured of most prompt and expensive reports according to one of these gentlemen. Joseph Clark, a publicity expert for the three forces, is in England as chief of the information bureau, to build up a new news system. He is a fine young gentleman personally, but a mint of money is being spent like water. I think, however, that he goes too far.
What sums of money have been spent by this bureau since the start, I do not know, in payment for drawing-room accommodation, compartment accommodation, railway fares, hotel expenses, and expenditures for meals and refreshments, both within and without Canada. I believe also the government is making a great mistake. C-onsorship should have been abolished long ago. Why should friends of this country be misled? Are we to follow the dictatorships in that respect? Of what use is this censorship? Some hockey reporters who have never had any training in defence matters, or foreign affairs, are made censors. They are engaged to act as censors and to control the work of
Public Accounts

skilled newspapermen in our own press gallery. I can tell you this, that that is one thing that is going on.
Then, I hold, in my hand a pamphlet entitled "Dieppe", by Bob Bowman. The radio corporation is just as bad as the information bureau. We are told in this pamphlet that "our losses in Dieppe were not in vain". This was issued after the Dieppe raid and circulated throughout Canada. As opposed to that we have Mr. Churchill's speeches in the House of Commons on September 8 and on Armistice day, last November, in which he gave full information.
How long this will go on I do not know, but it is going on now. And1 I contended at the first meeting of the public accounts committee that the expenditures in connection with the victory loan campaigns should be before the committee. I believe that in war time certain principles are fundamental; namely, that the country should come first and that nothing should stand in the way of the public good and the public safety. I have always believed that the possession of private property is a vital factor at any time, and I suggest that all this talk about what is to come after the war is over is a waste of time, because it will never come true. Neither victory nor any amount of planning will ever bring about the millennium.
I believe the set-up of this information bureau is all wrong and that it should be changed immediately or abolished, along with the censorship regulations. We do not hear very much from these publicity and information bureaux or the radio commission about Empire day; there is hardly a word to be heard about this empire. Are we to allow it to go by the board so far as these publicity boards and radio commissions are concerned? I say no, and I believe the time has come when they must reform their ways or be abolished in the interests of the, country.
There are many other matters to which I might refer, but I think I should conclude because there are others who will want to take part in this debate. I believe there are matters in connection with these aeroplane plants which should be examined by the public accounts committee. If something is not done before the war comes to a close it will be found almost impossible to obtain reasonably speedy settlement of the accounts due business men in connection with these aeroplane and munition factories when the "cease work" comes. There should be a standard form of accounting, and all that sort of thing. So far as the soldiers 
are concerned, they are nowhere. They are working over there for $1.30 a day, including some very fine newspaper men, while we are carrying on this publicity and censorship here.

and examined1 the public accounts. I should have pointed out that there was a Tory government in power at that time. The public accounts committee met in each of the five years that government was in power.

I do not know very much about the wartime information board, but I do know this, that right from the inception of the war the critics of the government were very industrious in pointing out that Canada's war effort was not being properly portrayed, not being understood, not being given sufficient publicity. Speaker after speaker in 1939, 1940 and 1941, and even last year, pointed out that our war effort was not understood in Great Britain, not understood in the United States. The government made many efforts to meet what was a difficult situation, and finally the wartime information board was set up under Mr. Vining, whom I do not know, but who I understand is a distinguished newspaper man in Canada with a more than national reputation. Mr. Vining headed the board until he had to retire on account of ill health. He was later succeeded by Mr. John Grierson.
Statements have been read into Hansard with regard to expenditures and also with regard to salaries of the wartime information board. Some of these salaries may be out of line; I do not know whether they are or not. The one that was held up to us for criticism was that of Mr. Casey, who I understand is a national, if not an international publicist. He managed the publicity for the New York World's Fair and also for Mr. Wendell Willkie in the 1940 presidential campaign. His occupation with the wartime information board in New York was only of a few months' duration, and he resigned, I understand, to take the responsible position of chief publicity agent for the Grand Old Party in the United States. The Grand Old Party is the nearest counterpart in the United States to the Conservative party in Canada, or the Progressive Conservative party, if they so desire.
Mr. Grierson made a statement indicating that some adjustments were necessaiy and that he had made those adjustments. But he has not had sufficient time to outline and put into effect any changed programme he may have in mind. Be that as it may, the opposition have a course of action open to them. If they think the matter is of sufficient importance and they have the knowledge which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie -King) said was a prerequisite, they can move a substantive motion for the appointment of a special committee to examine into the matter. Second, they can support the motion to appoint the war expenditures committee and have this item referred to it. Third, they can join with other members of the house in relieving the public accounts committee of its responsibility to examine into the public accounts and the auditor general's report, but until such time as that is done I for one intend to vote for the motion and to get along with our work as rapidly as possible and put ourselves in a position to carry out that reference, namely, to examine and investigate the public accounts and the auditor general's report, and make a report thereon.

I would remind the house that the people of this country have just subscribed over one and a quarter billion dollars. Like other members of the house I offered my services to the war finance committee in my constituency, and during the Easter recess I was introduced in the various communities by citizens who did not share my political views. In each community I tried as well as I could to impress upon the people the importance of cooperating in the victory loan. I answered some questions in the minds of the people as to whether we have any extrava-

gance in Canada, whether any public funds are being wasted. I told them that it was hardly possible with an expenditure of five and a half billion dollars in the present year that there would not ibe some extravagances, some moneys wasted, but I said that I did not know of a single member of the cabinet who would not welcome information from members of parliament or people in the country as to specific cases of waste.
I think it is disturbing to see this debate continue for two afternoons now, with supporters of the government stubbornly refusing to have this particular question referred to the public accounts committee. I have personally a great deal of respect for the work which has been done by the wartime information board. I believe this debate does a great injustice to the board. While the points of procedure which are raised are understood by members of this house, the people of Canada find it difficult to understand why an expenditure of half a million dollars is not referred to a properly constituted committee of the house for full consideration. I believe that some of the men who are trying to bring to the attention of the people of Canada, the United States and Great Britain the problems of Canada and its part in this conflict are doing an essential job.
A return was brought down on March 29 containing the names of some of the dollar-a-year men who are giving their services. I do not propose to discuss these men; but the salaries which are being paid to them by their companies, would, I imagine, make some of the salaries paid to employees of the wartime information board look like chicken-feed. Those who are making a contribution by the use of the pen are doing an important and essential job. The wartime information board could very well come before a parliamentary commission, give in public the story of what they are doing, and answer satisfactorily many of the questions which hon. members might feel like asking. But the refusal to have this information given in public, the determination to have the investigation referred to a committee which will sit in camera, while the people are kept in suspense for six months or a year in regard to this particular question, is very bad, coming just at the conclusion of the magnificent response which was made by the people of this country to the war loan.
I appeal to ministers to accept, even at this stage, the amendment of the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Black), let us get on with the business of the house, and take a chance on the conduct of the wartime information board being above board and that the money which has been spent can be accounted for in a satisfactory manner.

Listening to the arguments of hon. members opposite, one would be inclined to conclude, if one listened only to them, that the government is refusing investigation of public-expenditures and is trying, as someone said, to-hide extravagance from the eyes of the public. It seems to me that most of this long debate has been outside the question altogether as I understand it. In my humble opinion this matter of public expenditure can be divided, as the acting Prime Minister explained yesterday, into two grounds, which cover the whole matter of public expenditure. First, there is the public accounts committee, which is a committee of the house ready to sit during the session and to which is referred and can be referred any expenditure contained in the auditor general's report. Second, there is the war expenditures committee, which was formed, if I remember well, upon the suggestion of the then leader of the official opposition, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). These two committees can investigate to the last dollar any expenditure which the government is making in this country. Consequently all this long debate about this thing not being done and this other thing being evaded by the government seems to me wholly useless, because ail the expenditures of the government can be investigated by these two committees. Why, -then, so long a discussion?
One argument which has been advanced is that the committee on war expenditures sits in camera. I am not sure, but perhaps, if the amendment of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) were carried, the first ones to regret it would be the members of the-Conservative party. Since the beginning of the war we members of the Liberal party have been advised and notified officially that during the war there shall be no political interference-in war expenditures, war appointments or military promotions. We have followed that instruction strictly and faithfully since the beginning. What has happened? Due to our obedience to the order of the government all these boards, the civil service, and the commissions, are flooded with Conservatives, and with many citizens adhering to the other opposition parties. Therefore, if the public accounts committee is authorized, as the amendment requests, to make investigation of expenditures, it will be of expenditures and extravagances by Tories in these commissions and filling these other appointments. I repeat that the first to regret it will be those who are trying so strenuously to obtain it.

but I do not take a back seat to him so far as courage is concerned. I consider it my duty to speak of what I believe to be in the interests of this country, and the people whom I represent.

But that 'member was the hon. member for Halton, who attended the meeting of the public accounts committee the day before yesterday, took a front seat at the committee table, and arose without the decency of asking the permission of the chair to appear either as a witness or as anything else, and challenged the statements of other committee members who suggested that certain documents and information should be produced before the committee. He went into some detail this afternoon in connection with the record of attendance of some of my colleagues before the war expenditures committee. But, during that time, irrespective of what was said to-day by the hon. member for Regina'City (Mr. McNiven), about putting first things first, let me say that while I was present, not one member of that committee who supported him suggested one item we should investigate.	*
I had no intention of putting all these details before the house, until the hon. member spoke this afternoon. He continued at considerable

length -with respect to the war expenditures committee. It was pointed out by the minister who has been leading the house for the last two days, that this matter should be referred to the war expenditures committee. Other hon. members have supported him in arguing that that certainly is the place to make investigations. I think it is fairly generally realized by the public that at other sessions the war expenditures committee was composed of eighteen government supporters, four members from this party, one from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party and one from the Social Credit group.
As to what we might investigate in that committee, I believe I have before me the last report of the war expenditures committee, dated January 27, il&43. This afternoon one hon. member asked the hon. member for Halton to say something about the Gimli air field, and as to why that should be investigated in secret. This last report will give hon. members some idea of how far we could get before the war expenditures committee, which, as I pointed out yesterday, has not sat in over six months. This report states:
In regard to the Gimli air field controversy raised by the Winnipeg Tribune, their solicitor has indicated that in the opinion of his principals a public inquiry should be held to accurately determine the value of the land acquired at Gimli; that expert witnesses should be called for and against the correctness of the actual purchase price paid for the land, in fact, that nothing short of an inquiry in the nature of a trial in public to determine the actual value of the land purchased would satisfactorily dispose of the matter. The subcommittee has fully considered the scope of its authority and its reference by parliament. The Canadian war expenditures committee is patterned after the British Avar expenditures committee, and Avhile its powers are in part someAvhat Avider than the powers conferred upon the British war expenditures committee, yet in the main its duty is to check Canada's war expenditures for the purpose of ensuring that all proper safeguards are set up in regard to the expenditure of public money. It is not
the duty of this subcommittee to supplant the responsibility either of the public accounts committee or the civil courts. This subcommittee does not express any opinion as to the need for further inquiry.
