The house resumed at eight o'clock. PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

Mr. Speaker, just before the dinner recess I was referring to the January 27 report of the war expenditures committee and to the implication in it that a certain matter which had been under investigation by it might more properly be investigated by the public accounts committee. I shall have a great deal more to say about that on a more appropriate occasion in this house.
The point I wish to make now is that we had the implication in that report of the war expenditures committee-I believe the chairman of the committee at that time was the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver)

that this matter might more properly be investigated by the public accounts committee, but yesterday we had the minister who was leading the house pointing out on two occasions that the wartime information board and all the publicity work of the government might far
Public Accounts

better be investigated by the war expenditures committee. To use the language of the man on the street, I do not know where you could find any better example of passing the buck by responsible members of this government.
When the public accounts committee was given its terms of reference on March 8 I stated that I was very sorry that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had said that the government could not accept the amendment proposed at that time by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). I said that because from past experience I had an idea of what would happen in the future. I went on to cite certain debates that had taken place in the house and to point out that the Minister of Munitions and Supply had said that that particular matter should be investigated by the war expenditures committee. But when that question was raised in the war expenditures committee, the chairman said that the terms of reference would not permit of the matter being investigated. I pointed out that such procedure amounted to locking the door after the horse was stolen.. In other words, when we saw waste taking place we had no opportunity to investigate and prevent that waste until after a properly audited report had been tabled in this house. The Prime Minister interjected to say, "That is not correct." I then went on to point out exactly what he had said when the war expenditures committee was under discussion on previous occasions, and I indicated what I thought would happen in the future, which is precisely what is now happening in this debate.
I do not wish to take further time, but 1 hope that the government will see fit to accept the amendment proposed by my colleague the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). It is the least the public expect at a time like this. I do not want to repeat the arguments that have been so ably presented in concrete form by my colleagues, but before sitting down I would plead again with the members of the house to support the amendment in fairness to the taxpayers of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had an amendment moved to the motion for concurrence in the second report of the public accounts committee. The discussion on that motion took up considerable time, and after the amendment was declared out of order we had another proposed by the member for Yukon (Mr. Black). I should like to call to the attention of the house the wording of that second amendment. It reads:
That the said report be not now concurred in but that it be recommitted to the public accounts committee with instruction that they
fMr. J. A. Ross.]
have power to amend the same so as to recommend that said committee have power to investigate expenditures incurred for publicity or in relation thereto by wartime information board and by various governmental departments and boards, subsequent to March 31, 1942.
I have read that in order to call the attention of the house to the fact that there is no question about the power which the public accounts committee has to deal with matters of this kind, nor is there any question about the authority which the public accounts committee has to recommend different matters to this house. The public accounts committee has already exercised in the committee itself any authority or power which it had to deal with the very question which has been before this house during the last two days, and the position which the committee reached in that matter was given to the house just before the dinner recess by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven) when he stated that the public accounts had been referred to the public accounts committee and it was their first duty to examine into those accounts and to report back to the house their findings with regard to them. But while the committee were in the midst of considering the .public accounts which had been referred to them, there was a reference made to this house from the committee to the effect that another matter should be referred to the public accounts committee. That matter was referred to the public accounts committee. Upon that occasion a discussion took place in the house in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and others clearly pointed out what the powers of the public accounts committee are, the way in which those powers could be exercised and the extent to which matters could be referred to that committee. But after that particular matter was referred to the committee and was under consideration by them, some experiences were gained which were hinted at by the Prime Minister at the time the matter was referred to that committee. He said, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Regina City a few hours ago, that that reference to the committee was not to be taken as a precedent for referring to that committee everything about which complaint might be made in the press. As a result of that reference at that time we have had some experiences which I think it is well for us to keep in mind now.
I have had the privilege of travelling over a part of Canada since the committee considered the evidence of Mr. Thompson, and I was very much surprised to find that many of those things which were nothing more than rumours in connection with particular matters under consideration by the public accounts committee were looked upon by the public in

Public Accounts
certain parts of Canada as being truths. For example, I had the privilege of visiting an airport in a certain part of Canada, where a story which I had never heard even in Ottawa was circulating. One of the officers said to me, "I must take you into my office to show you my 31,500 rug". I said, "Have you got a $1,500 rug?" and he replied, "Come in and have a look at it. That is the story which is circulating around this community, and it is being talked about continually as a result of some of your investigations in Ottawa." I went in and found two little rugs, I imagine about 9 by 11J, which is one of the commercial sizes, lying side by side on the floor. The cost of those rugs, Mr. Speaker, was $37.50. Yet the story was circulating, growing out of the committee's investigation, that this rug had cost $1,500.
I should like to suggest to the house the method by which that kind of story got out. I picked up the morning paper in Ottawa during the committee's investigation-I had not been present in the committee-and I read a story which at first led me to believe that someone had purchased rugs at a cost of four or five hundred dollars apiece. That was in the newspaper headlines. But when I read the story carefully, the questions and answers being printed on the front page of the paper, I found that a member of the opposition who was questioning a witness before that committee had merely asked Colonel Thompson whether he had heard the story about the four and five hundred dollar rugs, and Colonel Thompson said, yes. The question was not followed farther than that, but by the asking of that question and by the manner in which the evidence was allowed to go out from that committee to the country the impression was given that four and five hundred dollar rugs had been purchased for office purposes. Of course when the facts were examined into, it was established that that was not the situation at all.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in peace time there is perhaps no great harm done by that kind of thing because the truth finally catches .up with the story, but in time of war, when we are putting on as we were putting on at that time a campaign to raise an enormous sum of money to equip our armed forces fighting overseas, it is a much more serious matter to have investigations of that kind going on and inquiries of that kind being made and statements of that kind going out to the public throughout the length and breadth of this country, particularly when they are not true.
I recite that only to say this, that we must be more or less careful in these times as to how inquiries are carried on.
An attempt has been made, since this discussion began, to leave the impression in this country that someone on the government benches, or some group on the government benches, or all the government, are opposed to an inquiry being made into charges which have been made with regard to overexpenditures of money or with regard to salaries being too high. Nothing has been said by any member of the government or by anyone speaking on this side of the house to indicate that there is any objection to proper inquiry being made into all expenditures in connection with all activities of the government, whether they have to do with the war or otherwise; and I think it should be made perfectly clear that all members on this side- and I think I can speak in this regard for members on the other side as well'-desire to have proper inquiry made into any expenditures of money about which, there is criticism or as to which there is any chance of there having been graft or something of that kind. I think I can say that everyone in the house, irrespective of party, is desirous of having that result. But we do take exception to items such as have appeared since yesterday in the press. I do not hold hon. members responsible for all that appears in the press by way of propaganda. When an hon. member, speaking yesterday to the other resolution, referred to his not being in favour of propaganda, I suggest to him that there is no more vile propaganda circulated in this country at any time than the kind of propaganda which appeared in the press this morning to the effect that members of the house, on the government side in particular, were obj acting to inquiries into expenditures made by the government or any of its officials. '
Well, the public accounts committee has power to examine into different matters. This house has the power to refer almost any kind of expenditure to the public accounts committee. The question was raised yesterday whether it was the best kind of procedure to take in making investigation into the kind of expenditure which we have under consideration. Some hon. members- I would think, members on both sides-may be of opinion that the expenditure might be properly inquired into in the public accounts committee; and a great many-I hope, some on both sides of the house- would have the opinion that it might be inquired into more properly and to better advantage in the war expenditures committee. I happen to be one of those in the latter group, who think that the best results
Public Accounts

could be obtained, with any inquiries which might be made, through a reference to the latter committee. When that suggestion is made the. question is raised as- to when that committee is to be appointed; and this afternoon, when the acting leader of the government was attempting to give some opinions with regard to that matter to the house, objection was taken to his doing so on a technical point, and probably the technical objection was quite properly taken. But I suggest that it has been the custom in this house, when any hon, member has been addressing the house, if it happens to be a member on this side and the leader of the op,position rises in his place and desires to make a correction regarding anything that he has said, or make an explanation regarding anything he has said, for hon. members to take their seats and allow him to do so. On the other hand, when at any time the Prime Minister has found it advisable ,t-o rise in his place and ask for the privilege of making an explanation with regard to any matter of that kind, it has always been customary for hon. members on the other side to take their seats for the moment and allow that explanation to be made. I submit that it would have been only proper for that to have been done this afternoon when the acting leader of the house was attempting to make that explanation. But, Mr. Speaker, that was not permitted at that time; and because it was not permitted, there are a few questions which I think might be dealt with in the few moments I intend to speak.
One of them has to do with the question as to when a committee of this kind-that is, a war expenditures committee-could be appointed. It has been appointed on two previous occasions, I believe, and appointed as a result of representations made in the press across Canada, by hon. members from the other side of the house, and representations which were concurred in by hon. members on this side. This year there has been on the order paper for a considerable time-the date on the order paper is February 24-a motion in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King):
That a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, and that notwithstanding standing order 65 the committee shall consist of twenty-four members, as follows.
The point I wish to make is that there is a motion on the order paper, standing under

the name of the Prime Minister, placed there on February 24, which provides for the very thing which has been diseussed here during the last two days. It provides for a select committee "to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war." In other words, the committee is to be set up for the purpose of doing exactly the thing which we are being asked on this occasion to submit to the public accounts committee. I do not think there was any doubt in the minds of hon. members on the opposition side of the house, when notice was given of this motion, that any matter such as that which we are discussing now ought to be brought to the attention of that committee when the proper time came. The Prime Minister, when he was discussing this matter in the house earlier, stated, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, what the position of himself and the government was with regard to that matter. On May 10, 1943, as reported in Hansard, at page 2508, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar put this question to the Prime Minister:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he will endeavour some time this week to arrange for the setting up of the war expenditures committee. The session is getting on.
The answer given by the Prime Minister was:
I should not like to enter into the reasons which have made it impossible to reach that particular item on the agenda before this, but certainly almost every time the government has moved to get on with some of its most important legislation there have been interruptions, for one reason or another. Other matters or measures have been brought up which have taken up a considerable amount of time. I understand the resolution referred to by my hon. friend is one that it is expected will take up some considerable time in discussion. In that event I think it should stand over until we have completed the measure which the Minister of Finance has introduced with respect to war supplies and also the war appropriation bill.
There could not be anything much clearer than that. Members have known for some time that just as soon as these two discussions are out of the way it has been the intention of the government and of the Prime Minister to have this committee named and have it constituted so that those matters which should be referred to it might be submitted. Members of the house know, too, that during this week the Prime Minister has been in Washington attending one of the most important meetings associated with the war which has been called

Public Accounts
since the beginning of the war, and being at that meeting he must of course give his entire time and attention to what is taking place there. Hon. members know also that last evening the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) was called to the same conference and along with him some of the important officials who know a great deal about matters having to do with defence. I am sure the house will agree with me that this is not the time to be discussing the matter which has been before us yesterday and again the whole of to-day to the present moment. This matter can be discussed to much greater advantage when the Prime Minister returns and when we have an opportunity of giving consideration to those questions which hon. members have been discussing during the past few days.
It is within the knowledge of the house that this committee is to be set up for the purpose of doing the very thing which hon. members have been saying ought to be done by somebody, and doing it in what the government considers to be the proper manner and, I am sure, in the manner in which most of the people of Canada would regard as proper by the war expenditures committee, operating in such a way as will be satisfactory to members of the house generally.
During the discussion to-day some other statements have been made to which I think some reference should be made. For instance, it has been stated that the wartime information board has been spending a great deal of money and that, because it has been doing so, some investigation should be made into its activities. While no one on this side of the house has raised any objection to the expenditures made by this board being examined into, it is well that when information is going out from the house as to expenditures, correct information should be placed on the record; and in order that we might establish what the relationship is of expenditures in connection with this board to the expenditures of similar boards set up elsewhere, I think I should place on the record the amount which has been expended by this board during the time it has been in office, and during the rest of the year by the bureau of public information

the amount that was spent during the twelvemonth period. In order to do so I should like to indicate the total expenditure in Canada under the two organizations during the fiscal year, and to state also what the expenditures have been in the United States and in Great Britain.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that no minister of the crown has defended the expenditures of the
board, and he went on to say that the only person who had defended them was the chairman of the board, in a press report which he made. Well, if no minister has defended the expenditures of the board up to the moment, I intend to do so now. In the first place, I wish to remind the house again that this board was demanded by the press. It was demanded by members of the opposition over the months of the war prior to the time it was set up, and in making those demands the then leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) expressed himself quite clearly on July 22, 1942, as reported at page 4517 of Hansard, as follows:
Mr. Vining occupies an important position in the industrial and commercial life of Canada. He was appointed, as I understood it, to survey the situation with relation to our publicity in the United States-a very important subject, and one which has not received the attention it should have received in the long months that this country has been at war. He was sent down there, as I understand it, for a definite purpose. He has made a report. It must be of a constructive character, and unless there is something highly confidential in it, it should be tabled.
There are two things of importance in that statement. The first is the extent to which the then leader of the opposition praised the man who made the report, and the second is the anxiety which he showed that that report should be acted upon at the earliest possible moment and that something should be done to improve, as he thought, the matter of handing information not only to this nation but to the great country to the south of us. And he had confidence that any finding which was made by Mr. Vining would be helpful to the government of the day. That might be looked upon as something of an official stand taken by the then leader of the opposition in this house, and I think it expresses, in as few words as it can be expressed, the attitude which had been taken by members of the apposition from different groups as well as the attitude which had been taken by a considerable part of the press throughout Canada down to the time the board was appointed.
When the board was appointed with Mr. Vining as chairman it proceeded to make appointments. I have noticed criticisms of those appointments in the press, and I am not in a position to answer them. I doubt if members in this house on either side are in a position to answer those criticisms, and I doubt if the members who do not know whether those criticisms are justified or not, and are only looking for information, -would want these matters discussed in public until there was some further information as to whether the salaries were justified or not. It is not sufficient for

Public Accounts

me or for a newspaper to say that we have a certain man employed whom they paid only $2,500 and that, therefore, when the government hire him and pay him $5,000 they are paying him too much. I have known of people who were drawing $2,500 who were worth $5,000, and I have known of people who were drawing $5,000 who were not worth $2,500. The situation is that some people have to find their groove before they show their real worth. I have not any doubt that some of the men who are occupying these positions to-day, and drawing the salaries which were placed before the house this afternoon, are earning their money; and I have not any reason for believing that they are not all earning it. I might have some reason for wanting to find out whether they are all earning it or not, and I would want to find that out by justifiable means, and by means which were likely to get the best results.
But usually when we are looking for trouble in the matter of expending money we try to find out some place where an enormous amount of money is being spent, an amount which is out of all proportion to that which somebody else is spending for the same job. Therefore I should like to make the comparison I spoke about a few minutes ago. The expenditure of the wartime information board, plus the expenditures of the bureau of public information for the last fiscal year amounted to approximately $1,600,000. Well, that is even a greater sum of money than has been discussed in this house. Hon. members have been talking about an expenditure of half a million dollars. But the expenditure for this purpose during the financial year-and the accounts are not quite all in-by the wartime information board and the bureau of public information was approximately $1,600,000.
Let us look at the expenditures in Great Britain for the same purpose. British Hansard of July 7, 1942, records that the estimated expenditure in Great Britain for this purpose was $38,270,000, as against our $1,600,000. The United States office of war information spent $35,847,000, and the inter-American set-up spent an additional $14,000,000, making a total of $49,847,000. The British, with a population less than four times that of Canada, spent twenty-four times as much money. And the United States, with a population twelve or thirteen times our population, spent thirty-one times as much money as we do, on a similar activity.
And- then someone has said in this house that Great Britain investigated all such matters, when asked to do so. I submit to the house that on a very considerable part of

these expenditures, if not all of them, Great Britain has never permitted-and particularly during war time-an investigation such as has been1 discussed in the house during the last two days.
I might say that Canada might still be charged with neglecting war information, as she was during the first two years of the war, if the matter of expenditures of money alone, as compared with expenditures in other countries for similar purposes, is to be the basis upon which we are to arrive at a conclusion. If it was a proper thing to have said two years ago that it was not good for Canada to be spending so much less money than they were spending in Great Britain; and if it was not a good thing for Canada to be spending so much less than they were spending in the United States, then it still must be a bad thing for Canada to be spending only $1,600,000 when Great Britain is spending $38,270,000 and the United States, $49,847,000.

Will the minister
permit a question? I wonder if, instead of giving us a comparison in populations, he will give us a comparison of the national budgets of each country. That will be a fairer comparison.

I do not think we
would be very far out, if we did that. The Minister of Finance is here, and he knows that part of the subject better than I do.

I think it would be more
favourable.

Some one says to me
that in that event they could spend a hundred thousand dollars for a rug.
And most likely would, too.

The point is this: Comparisons have been made in the house in recent weeks, and1 I imagine they will be made in the days ahead of us, showing up Canada's expenditures for war purposes, in relation to the expenditures of other countries. I believe it has been agreed long ago that our expenditures compare most favourably with those of any other country in the world, either within or outside the allied countries.
My purpose in rising was to obtain a comparison between our expenditures on publicity, and our total war expenditures. I was not suggesting an expenditure as interpreted by the minister.

It will work out much the same way. The comparison we have always made of our total expenditures with those of Great Britain has been a comparison

Public Accounts
of our expenditures on a per capita basis with the total expenditures of Britain on a per capita basis. And if, on a per capita basis, we are spending such a small amount for information, as compared with Great Britain, then I think that answers the question the hon. member has put as to the relationship between those expenditures and the total budget. It will be about the same relationship as that I have indicated to the house as between Canadian, British and United States expenditures on publicity.
I should like to deal with just one other matter in this connection, and that has to do with some of the remarks of some speakers, referring largely to what I said yesterday in another debate. I shall refer to what they said to-day in this debate. In making reference to that matter the same word was used to-day by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) as was used last night by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) in introducing his amendment. It was suggested I had said to the house yesterday that the public accounts committee is set up as a result of action on the part of the opposition. That, of course, is evidently not the situation. All the committees in the house are set up upon motion by [DOT] the government, and the public accounts committee is set up in exactly the same way. But it has been a new experience in my thirty years of public life to have an opposition, or groups in the opposition, deny interest in the most effective instrument placed in the hands of those in opposition to the government to examine into expenditures made by the government. Anyone who denies that the public accounts committee is of greater interest, in so far as membership in the house is concerned, to the members who sit in opposition than to those who sit on the government side of the house is denying, let me say, the effectiveness of the best instrument that has been placed in the hands of oppositions with which to check the financial activities of the government itself.
It is all very well to say that the public accounts committee is set up for the benefit of the public. It is. But if the opposition of the day refuse to use that public accounts committee in the manner in which it was intended to be used, and turns it into a fishing expedition, to see if they can find out something about something else, then all I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is that they do not realize what, has been placed in their hands.
This was brought out effectively this afternoon by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven). He said that I told only part of the story yesterday. I referred to the fact that we always had public accounts committees meeting when we were sitting in opposition in another house-and we had. Then he
72537-18H
went on to say that as a result of those-examinations none of the government party was elected in the next election. But he neglected just one thing. The hon. gentleman who has been most insistent in raising matters of this kind in this house was the leader of the opposition in that province for a period of time between that election and the next one. He ran an election, and he did not elect anyone, either. There was a very good reason-for it. We had investigations by the public accounts committee. Not only that, but during the five years we were, out of office the government had a commission which inquired into all the activities of the previous government during the twenty-four years we had been in power; and the worst they were able to report with regard to the period during which I had something to do with the government was that when we did not employ a policeman, I did not tell his wife all the reasons why we did not employ him.
I would submit that investigations of that kind do not get us very far. The people of the country eventually take the measure of persons who carry on such investigations. When they have an opportunity to express themselves through the ballot they usually are not very far wrong in their expressions of opinion. It does not help this country to have stories going round with regard to expenditures in connection with information. If we do not spend enough, we are criticized; if it is thought we spend too much, we are criticized, with no effort made to place all the facts before the people but only an attempt to disorganize any activities which are being carried on or to create discontent among our people at a time when we are attempting to raise enormous sums of money in order to carry on the war effort.

Mr. Speaker, in order to give your ears relief from listening to my miserable English, I know you will be glad to hear that I intend to address the Chair in my mother tongue.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I have heard with much interest the speeches delivered this afternoon by hon. members from both sides of the house on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). All those speeches were undoubtedly most interesting, but, the one which especially held my attention until the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke a few minutes ago, was the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver). Before commenting on that speech, I wish to refer to the challenge directed by the Minister of Agriculture a few moments ago to those who criticize the extravagant expenditures of the government information board. The Minister of Agriculture seemed to dare the opposition to prove to the satisfaction of the government that a single dollar was improperly spent by the information board. This afternoon, on the same topic, the hon. member for

Halton stated that not one member had made a definite and positive charge against that government information board. The hon. member also rebuked opposition members who criticize the government and demand that a committee be appointed to inquire into public accounts and especially into the administration of the information board. He took the Conservative party to task for spending huge sums all over the country for advertising purposes; he claimed moreover that such sums would have been incomparably more useful to Canada and the allied nations if they had been put into the government's treasury to support our war effort. That may be all very well, and I have not the slightest intention to rise in defence of the Conservative party; far from it. Neither is it necessary for me to say that I have no longer any interest in that party.
The reason why I refer to that part of the speech delivered by the hon. member for Halton is that if it were shown, through an inquiry into public accounts, that the Liberal party uses the public funds for its own propaganda across Canada and especially in the province of Quebec, that party would be in a much worse situation than the Conservative party could be, for the latter, at least, uses its own funds.
I hold in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a copy of . the Montreal newspaper Le Devoir, dated Tuesday, May 18, 1943, and I notice therein under the signature of Omer Heroux an article entitled "II est temps de crier halte-la!" -the time has come to call a halt! The caption goes on as follows:
An account showing that the dominion wartime information board is using for propaganda purposes in favour of Mr. Godbout funds earmarked for war purposes-an action that is neither conceivable nor even quite clever- an appeal to the staunchest supporters of the provincial Prime Minister.
As the article is somewhat lengthy I shall give a summary of it. According to Mr. Omer Heroux, the French-language newspapers in Montreal received1 on May 13, in an envelope bearing the words "On His Majesty's Service-Information Board" the French translation of two articles, one of which was published in the Ottawa Evening Journal and the other a letter written from the Times correspondent. The letter from the Times correspondent and the article from the Ottawa Evening Journal were translated by the information board and sent to the French-language newspapers of the province of Quebec. And Le Canada of the day before yesterday, that is to say Monday, reproduced

the Ottawa Evening Journal's letter. One of these articles, translated into French, had the following titles:
Two states within the Canadian state

Quebec, a loyal province within the dominion -safeguarding of the French heritage.
This article deals, I believe, with the act recently introduced by the government of the province of Quebec, on compulsory education. Here is what it says:
Shrewd and honest, Mr. Godbout seems to have thoroughly understood the seriousness of the situation.
Then, in the letter to the Times'.
While giving proper consideration to wartime government problems, Mr. Godbout has done much to remedy political and economic uneasiness. He has crossed swords with those who advocate a kind of sectionalism in favour among Canadians, and at the risk of endangering his political career, he sought to establish that a Canadian confederation still presents the best solution for Quebec problems.
Political opinions are divided on the success of such an attitude; but everyone agrees that retaining Mr. Godbout in his position would be a major contribution to national unity.
Articles of that type are nothing more than electoral and party propaganda translated at government expense, that is at the expense of the national exchequer, by the wartime information board, and sent to Le Canada and other newspapers to be circulated through the province in the interests of a political party, as I said, a moment ago. If that is not a waste of public moneys, I wonder what could be called waste and what would constitute sufficient justification for voicing protests in this house.
Moreover, every morning, at eight o'clock, I listen to a CBC programme which, I think is entitled "Matutinal Elevations" on the French network. On that broadcast several times a week a certain gentleman from Quebec, who is a journalist, comments on current events, on the war and Catholic wartime problems. It so happens that most of his comments are in praise of the dominion and Quebec governments. I am deeply interested in listening to that gentleman's comments, but he has no right to carry on propaganda in favour of this or that party out of the public funds. We are told! that this programme broadcast every morning at eight o'clock on the French network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, is also paid by the information board. It is this same service that translated the letter eulogizing Mr. Godbout, and all this is being carried on in the province of Quebec at our expense.
Hon. members demanding that a committee be formed to investigate public accounts
find, as this session progresses, not only that they are within their rights but that they are also discharging a duty in doing so. If only the government afforded members an opportunity to investigate public accounts and the manner in which public moneys are spent, we might be able to prove to the minister of Agriculture and to the public-spirited member for Halton that more than one dollar is wrongly spent by the wartime information board. From all parts, and when I say from, all parts of the house I mean from every province, and from all parts of the country, is steadily heard the complaint that the information service is being used for electoral propaganda.
If the government had any regard for dignity and honour, and did not forever seek shelter under pretence of war conditions, with the constant claim that it is inadvisable to dwell upon this or that matter or to criticize the government, the resulting impression would not be so bad throughout the country. I submit that such a pure and unsullied government should agree to this inquiry in order to justify its policy. I want to do them a favour when I suggest that they scotch all those rumours which, it is said, are proving so detrimental and harmful to the best interests of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I support the amendment of the hon. member for Yukon and shall vote accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, as I have had1 but scant opportunity to address the house, I beg your indulgence while I do so to-night, even without preparation, for it is not without some gratification that I take this occasion to reply to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy).
The house is now considering the advisability of affording its members, either from the government side or from the opposition, to inquire into the government expenditures with regard to wartime information. It might be claimed in certain quarters that the government have been niggardly in this connection, while others may claim that the government have been extravagant. For my part, as a French Canadian, speaking as a representative of the province of Quebec, I feel no hesitation in stating that the government have not been guilty of extravagance in this regard and that, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, much more could have been spent for the purpose of enlightening the people and of explaining to them why we are at war, and why we should do our best to win the war. And when I hear speeches of the type just
Public Accounts

made by the hon. member for Gaspe, speeches such as have been delivered since the beginning of the session by a handful of Quebec members who seem to think that we are going too far in our war effort, I realize that theirs are the only discordant voices heard in this house. Indeed they are ever criticizing the war effort, opposing war measures, war propaganda in favour of our allies and the defence of Canada, and any measure in sup. port of those who are striving to regain their freedom. Indeed, the only voices so heard are unfortunately those of six of seven members from the province of Quebec. The government propaganda will never be too intensive, Mr. Speaker, if everyone in Canada, especially in the province of Quebec, is to be convinced that he should1 do his share as the majority of our citizens are doing. I realize how irksome it must be for certain members of this house when the only voices heard against the war effort in this parliament, nearly every day, are those of six or seven Quebec members, while more than fifty of the representatives of that province staunchly support the government, who want us to carry our share of the burden, to save our country, to save England, the fountain-head of the freedoms enjoyed in the province of Quebec and at the same time to save France, which we have not forgotten and which, if our hopes are realized, will be free again in the near future.
Last year we held a secret session. The country was upset by the news of a secret session to investigate the defence of the St. Lawrence river. Mr. Speaker, I state without any hesitation that this secret session was nothing but propaganda, but not of the helpful kind, not of the kind that promotes the interests of the united nations, but the interests of the hon. member for Gaspe. We have met in secret session to hear this hon. member who stated he had witnessed a few engagements from his home and who wished to inform the house that ships had been sunk in the St. Lawrence. Did he suppose that the hon. Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the hon. Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) were aware of this and took no interest in the defence of Canada and needed the hon. member for Gaspe to defend the country and the St. Lawrence? Mr. Speaker, I am not the member for Gaspe, but I represent the constituency of Montreal-Ste. Marie, bounded on 
the south by the river St. Lawrence. We have not yet seen any submarines; however, our sentiments for our great river are as deep as those of the hon. member for Gaspe and all the hon. members sharing his views who attempt to sabotage the earnest endeavours of the Liberal government, who with the help of the broad-minded hon. members from the other side of the house are making a real effort to beat the axis powers, Germany, Italy or Japan.
Speaking of propaganda, Mr. Speaker, Le Devoir has been quoted a short time ago. Would you allow me, regarding this newspaper, to express the views of well-thinking French Canadians in Quebec. Had the government done everything possible and discharged their responsibilities in full, this newspaper would have been shut down long since and its distribution in the province of Quebec suspended.
They say the government is spending too much money on propaganda. Not more than a year ago this Notre Dame street newspaper, Le Devoir, was distributed in Montreal by its friends, the members of the Bloc Populaire, those people who claim for their province a greater love than the Liberal members for Quebec, in Montreal and elsewhere, in order to carry out their sabotaging attempts more easily, dn order to' be in a better position to belittle the people who, accepting their responsibilities, wished to assist the government, it was said, over and over again, that young curly-haired Englishmen, fugitives from the British Isles with the connivance of the government, were taking refuge in Montreal and were being sheltered at the Viger hotel. And while Le Devoir, while pseudo-patriots of the Bloc Populaire were victimizing the Liberal members who were faithful to their duty, we were called " sheep," as they said, attempting to protect these curly-haired Englishmen who had run away from the British Isles to seek refuge in Montreal. An investigation was held. What were its findings? These young curly-haired Englishmen that we, supporters of the government, were protecting, turned out to be sailors of the merchant fleet, Mr. Speaker. Their ships had been sunk on the Atlantic; they had been rescued and brought to Montreal to find shelter, food and clothing while awaiting to be assigned new berths on ships that would take them back to the Atlantic ocean where the Germans were still lurking to blast their ships to the bottom, possibly with their crews.
Friends of Le Devoir on the other side of this house would have these people as English youths who had fled from their country, whilst

Public Accounts
we looked upon them as patriots for whom we could provide shelter in the Viger hotel. Had we been provided with information such as could have been made available, had more money been spent for that purpose, it would not have been possible to poison the minds of the people as did or attempted to do some hon. members, and as they are still attempting to do, not for the security of the country nor of the province nor of the St. Lawrence, sir, but in order to save their own party.
This newspaper, Le Devoir, has been quoted as criticizing the Liberal government for their use of the information service in favour of Mr. Godbout. Mr. Ggdbout has no need of the information board. He is quite able to take care of himself. It is propaganda on the part of the government to quote Mr. Godbout, they say. The government, Canadians as a whole, be they Conservative, Liberal, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or Social Credit followers, every one with an allied victory to heart, can never quote Mr. Godbout too often, Mr. Speaker, as one who has fearlessly shouldered his responsibilities, spoken to the province of Quebec, taken a bold stand in the legislature and elsewhere and given his full and wholehearted support to our war effort. He did that for Canada, for Great Britain and for France. Moreover, had Le Devoir gone farther, it might have said that the government were using their propaganda office not only to extol the virtues of the Quebec prime minister but also to extol those of the spiritual leader of the province of Quebec and of Canada as a whole. If I have risen here to-night it is because I am proud of my province, I am proud of my leaders. It is also for the purpose of showing to people of this country and to the English-speaking members of this house, whatever their political affiliations may be, that the feelings of the province of Quebec are not voiced by the members who sit on the other side of this house, but by the members who have supported the government and the country's war effort. The true voice of Quebec is that of its spiritual leader, Cardinal Villeneuve, and also of its temporal leader, who heads the provincial government, the honourable Mr. Godbout. Thanks to these two distinguished men, we from the province of Quebec, as well as other French-Canadian members from other provinces, are able to sit here, Mr. Speaker, and hold our heads high among our English-' speaking fellow members.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to recall a memory which is still vividly impressed on my mind. A short while ago, in this province of Quebec of which so much is said, where one wonders whether the mentality of the people is the
same as in the rest of Canada, a by-election was held in Outremont. The government candidate, who was later elected, was the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche). At one of his first meetings, in a district where the campaign against him had been most strenuous, fanatical partisans had been brought in from outside the constituency, from suburban Montreal1 districts, to pack the hall. These people had been brought into the hall to embarrass the candidate and the speakers. On the eve of this meeting, newspapers and the radio had broadcast the news of the fall of Toulon. These publicity mediums had feelingly recounted to the world the commendable behaviour of these French sailors who had chosen to scuttle their ships and risked going down with them rather than turn their navy over to the enemy, Germany. The people of this constituency, like everybody else, were greatly impressed by the happenings at Toulon. However, at this meeting, those of our citizens who enjoy equally catcalls and applause, seemed inclined to annoy the government candidate. There was trouble until a speaker, former conservative candidate in this same constituency and an outstanding member of the Montreal bar, took the floor. Veteran of the last war, a native of Brittany, his emotions probably reaching deeper because of his French birth, he related to the audience the events enacted at Toulon, emphasizing the self-denial of these Frenchmen who put their lives in jeopardy when scuttling their ships. Mr. Speaker, if I recall these happenings, it is because I am still greatly impressed, and because this illustrates well French-Canadian sentiment. The whole audience, whether opponent or friends, forgot their differences and, bound by their feelings and their thoughts to the speaker who had so vividly described this deed of valour to them, of a common accord sang "La Marseillaise".. Mr. Speaker, if I took the floor to-night, as, I am convinced the majority of the members for Quebec would like to do, it is because I hope that, when the bells of Quebec ring victory for the British, French and other allied armies, I wish that my children, my compatriots of Quebec, may also hail victory, for the success of the allied forces will mean victory for Canada, victory for Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, in spite of the length of time which has been occupied in this debate, there are very few observations I wish to make at this stage, because the debate seems to me to have covered such an enormous amount of territory-not all of it directly connected with
Public Accounts

the matter before the house-that I wish to draw the attention of the house back again to what I consider to be one or two of the salient points.
This evening I listened with close attention to the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). He appeared to me to devote so much care and so much vigour to the statements he made that it was evident his effort was necessary for the bolstering of the government's position. Unquestionably the object of the speech by the minister was to strengthen the position occupied by the government.
It may well be that the only difference between the government and the opposition in this matter is the question of the appropriateness of one committee or the other to which these expenditures should be sent for discussion. The government takes the view that the war expenditures committee is the proper one to discuss and delve into these questions. The opposition is of opinion that the public accounts committee would be more competent for the purpose. It is sitting to-day; it sat in this building this morning. On the other hand, the war expenditures committee has not sat for six months. The notice bringing it into being is on the order paper, and has been there for three months. In the last official reference to it there appeared to us to be no indication whatsoever that it was shortly coming into being. We prefer the public accounts committee for the purpose of this investigation.

Would the hon. member
say that that should apply equally to an inquiry into the expenditures, say, of the defence departments, or of the Department of Munitions and Supply?

I think in the course
of my remarks I shall be able to indicate that the public accounts committee is capable of the investigation of anything committed to it. I disagreed with the acting leader of the government when yesterday he advanced the view that the public accounts committee was not the correct body to which to send an investigation of this sort, because in the many years in which we have had public accounts committees it has dealt with routine matters. He pointed out that it has looked into questions brought before it through the report of the auditor general.
I was surprised to hear that statement, because it was not my conception of the public accounts committee. I remember that on more than one occasion, during my time in the house, matters which certainly did not

come under the auditor general's report were directed, by reference of the house, to the public accounts committee for investigation.
I turn to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, and find the following paragraph:
593. There shall be a standing committee, to be designated "the committee of public accounts" for the examination of the accounts showing the appropriation of the sums granted by parliament to meet the public expenditure.
There is no reference at all to the auditor general's report. The only reference made is to expenditures made at the direction of the house.
When I read the amendment of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) it appears to me that the matters mentioned therein are those very matters which might properly, and should be directed to the public accounts committee. I regret very much that the government has seen fit to oppose the amendment. I gather from the length of the debate it has allowed to take place that there is no intention on its part of acceding to the request of the opposition that the public accounts committee be given this task.
The amendment of the hon. member for Yukon refers not only to the wartime information board, which has cropped up so many times in this debate, but to certain other governmental and departmental expenditures as well. I think it is clear that expenditures which must be defrayed by moneys voted in this house might properly be considered by the committee on public accounts. And there is a question in my mind as to whether they might properly be considered by the committee on war expenditures.	,
To show that this amendment is in order, and is not likely to be ruled out of order, as was its predecessor, I would draw attention to paragraph 661 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, because I believe the amendment fully meets what is set forth in this paragraph:
When the motion is proposed the report may be referred back to the committee for further consideration or with instruction to amend the same in any respect. It is not competent for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision, hut if the house resolves that such reconsideration is necessary, the correct procedure is for the house to give the committee instructions which will enable it to consider the whole question again.
That is exactly what has occurred in regard to this matter so far as it refers to the expenditures of the wartime information board. The steering committee advised the public accounts committee. The public accounts committee did not accept the advice of the steering committee, but decided, by a majority vote, that

this matter should not be investigated. Therefore it cannot, for any reasons advanced in this house or elsewhere, change the decision at which it arrived. But the remedy lies with this house, and it is for that reason that the opposition has seen fit to bring this forward in the form of an amendment, for it is this house alone that can instruct the public accounts committee to make the investigation. speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take but a very short time at this stage of the debate, and my only reason for rising is that during the debate on the previous amendment a point of order was raised, and I felt that I should confine myself as far as possible to the terms of Your Honour's ruling. I want to make one or two observations, however, based upon some of the statements that have been made during the course of this debate. One hon. member on the government side made a statement which I think has been successfully dealt with_ already, but with which perhaps I should deal for a moment, namely, that the opposition has chosen an opportune time to stage this debate, while the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is in Washington. Perhaps hon. members know the situation well enough not to accept a statement of that kind, bearing in mind the procedure under which this motion was presented. The motion on which this amendment is founded has been standing on the order paper for a considerable time; as a matter of fact, some three or four weeks ago, before this motion actually came before the house, I had occasion to ask the chairman of the committee and the government to lay on the table a transcript of the evidence that had been taken up to the time of the presenting of the report. So that the matter has been standing for a considerable time; and if the mover, who was the chairman of the public accounts committee, chose to bring that motion before the house while the Prime Minister was absent, I do not think the opposition can be blamed. It was the time of his choosing, the time he picked himself; and if, as one hon. member said, there was any suggestion that the Prime Minister had been stabbed in the back, then he must have been stabbed in the back by his own friends, which is not an unusual thing in public life.
I had intended to say a few words in reply to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner); I jotted down the points he made, one by one;
but on looking them over, I think they generated more heat than light, and perhaps I will leave them as they are. However, with great honesty I wish to say that the government have asked us to understand their position, and I ask that the government understand ours. Had I been able to do so yesterday before the point of order was raised, I would have mentioned what I think is the most important point in the whole discussion. It has been said by many hon. members, particularly on the government side, that this is a question of whether the investigation of these expenditures should be conducted by one committee or the other. I recall that the hon. member for Chambly - Rouville (Mr. Dupuis) said, " hear, hear," when that statement was made from this side of the house. In other words, I think we are all agreed, or at least I am assuming we are agreed, that it is a question of whether the expenditures mentioned in the amendment of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) should go to the war expenditures committee on the one hand or to the public accounts committee on the other. This is the point in connection with which I want the government to understand our position; this is-why I asked the government to withdraw their opposition and to change their stand. I said in the house yesterday that the public would misunderstand the position of the government; to-day the Minister of Agriculture complains that according to the press this morning the public does misunderstand the position of the government. I warned the government yesterday on that very score.
Let me give the reason-it is a very simple one-why we ask that this matter should go to the public accounts committee? It is because the war expenditures committee cannot legally deal with it. If that is not a sufficient reason, I should like to be told a better one. Here is the situation, on a straight question of legality. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) is looking at me with great interest just now. I wish to be very careful in stating my grounds, for he may have to answer this point when I am through and I should like to give him every opportunity to do so if he can. Let us be clear about this, because it is the kernel of the whole discussion.
The amendment states:
. . . that said committee have power to investigate expenditures incurred for publicity or in relation thereto by wartime information board-
The argument of the government would be good if the amendment stopped there, but it is more comprehensive and asks for something else:
-and by various governmental departments and boards, subsequent to March 31, 1942.
Public Accounts

In other words, this amendment covers the wartime information board; it covers other wartime expenditures, but it covers expenditures in connection with peace-time matters as well. Any government expenditure on publicity is covered by this amendment. Let us see what would happen the very moment that broad order came before the war expenditures committee, to which the government suggests it should go. If my hon. friend will look at the order paper, at government notices of motion, he will see over what the war expenditures committee is to have jurisdiction, and he will find that the committee is confined to this:
... to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war.
It stops there. I suggest to my hon. friend that if he will look over the departments of government contained in the civil estimates, he will find a list of twenty-eight. I ask him by what stretch of the imagination that reference could apply to all of the civil departments of government? The government itself does not attempt it. Not one member of the government would rise in his place and say that every department was a wartime portfolio.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

If my hon. friend over there who was just about to interrupt me before I stopped him before he started will just wait a moment. If that had been the case, there would be nineteen parliamentary assistants instead of ten. Surely no one will argue that every department of the government is a war-time department. If they are not, then expenditures with respect to publicity in some departments cannot be dealt with toy the war expenditures committee.
I am making the point as simple as I can to-night. I want the government to understand our position. They have asked that I try to understand their position and I want them to understand my position as leader of this party. The reason why we want these matters to go to the public accounts committee is that it is the only committee that has a legal right to deal with the subjects covered by the amendment. That is why I ask the government to understand our position. I think the government have placed themselves in a wholly impossible position. If the subjects dealt with in the amendment are to be investigated, the government will find that they are barred legally from having certain parts of the expenditures dealt with by the

public accounts committee. What a hodgepodge! What a terrible position for the government to find themselves in! They would be legally barred from investigating the very things they have said should be referred to the war expenditures committee. Before my hon. friend puts himself in another impossible position, I suggest to him that he take advantage of this opportunity. I will not object if he rises in his place and asks the special privilege of withdrawing from this wholly involved position.
The question is-
May I ask the minister if he is going to withdraw.
I might say to my hon. friend that we have not the slightest intention of withdrawing.

Mr. Speaker, having moved the amendment I should like to say a few words. I do not mind admitting that I did not expect that this amendment would be productive of such a prolonged debate. First, I wish to assure the house that nothing was further from my mind when moving this amendment than to be unfair to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I offered my amendment to the motion to adopt the report of the public accounts committee on the day in which the chairman of that committee moved the adoption of the report. I had no option as to when my amendment would be moved. I moved it only because another amendment had been ruled out of order.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) upon the cleverly worded political speech which he delivered to the house this evening. I enjoyed it. To my mind we do not have enough such speeches in this house. It reminded me of old times, and I am sure the Minister of Mines and Resources '(Mr. Crerar) will agree with me when I say that if we had more such speeches this would be a better house. The Minister of Agriculture quoted the government notice of motion which stands on the order paper in the name of the Prime Minister. I shall quote only part of it, as follows:
That a select committee he appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war.	.
Note the words, "services directly connected with the war." The power of the committee as to what expenditures can be examined by it is limited by those words. If the expenditures of the wartime information board were exclusively for the defence services and for other

Public Accounts
services directly connected with the war, the argument of the Minister of Mines and Resources, now leading the house, and of the Minister of Agriculture, that the expenditures of this board should be more properly examined by the war expenditures committee might be sound. But the expenditures of the wartime information board are not limited to expenditures for the defence services and for other services directly connected with the war.

Every dollar expended by the wartime information board is voted under the war appropriation bill and arises directly out of the war, and consequently it would be included in the motion that stands in the name of the Prime Minister.

It may be voted as a war item, but it is not expended by the wartime information board for the defence services and for other services directly connected with the war. The minister and members of the house may ask me why I make that statement and upon what it is founded. If the house will bear with me for a few moments, I shall give it information about the policy of the wartime information board which to me is positively astounding. I desire to quote from the first issue I have ever seen of a magazine called The Gospel Witness.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members may not laugh so loudly when I am finished. I ask them to reserve their levity until I have completed my remarks. I think all members of this house, no matter what their religious beliefs may be or what their political adherence may be, will agree with me when I am through. I quote:
Last week a subscriber of The Gospel Witness forwarded to this office a four-page pamphlet entitled "Nouvelles Catlioliques"-

I have allowed the hon. gentleman to continue but I should like him to quote to me the rule under which he feels he is entitled to reply and speak a second time when he has already moved the amendment.
I understood that a member moving an amendment, which amounts to a resolution, has a right to close the debate.

Standing order 43
provides:
(1) No member may speak twice to a question except in explanation of a material part of his speech which may have been misquoted or misunderstood, but then he is not to introduce any new matter, and no debate shall be allowed upon such explanation.
(2) A reply shall be allowed to a member who has moved a substantive motion, but not to the mover of an amendment.
I am afraid, therefore, the hon. member has not the right to speak a second time in reply.

speechtext: Mr. G. J. McILRAITH (Ottawa West) moved the first reading of bill No. 67 (from the senate) respecting the Canada North-West Land Company Limited.

subtopic: THE CANADA NORTH-WEST LAND COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to explain this bill?

subtopic: THE CANADA NORTH-WEST LAND COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill is to reduce the qualifications required for directors of the Canada North-West Land Company Limited. The company was incorporated by chapter 88 of the statutes of 1893. The provision dealing with the qualifications of directors is to be found in section 8 of that act. and reads as follows:
The qualification of a member of the board shall be the holding in his own right of shares in the company of the nominal value of at least five thousand dollars.
By an amending act of 1903 provision was made for the liquidation in certain circumstances of the assets of the company, the distribution of the assets and the redemption of the stock. There has been since that date a substantial liquidation of the assets and distribution of the assets, with the result that it is now very difficult to have shareholders holding a sufficient capital stock qualification to become directors. Consequently the present bill is brought forward with the purpose of reducing the qualification to one hundred shares of the capital stock of the company.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on the matter of farm wages and the farm labour situation in Canada at the present time. The other day the Minister of National Defence stated that the situation in regard to man-power was tight. I should say that the situation in regard to man-power on the farms of Canada has been tight for some time, and if we are to get the increased production that will be necessary to fill the orders we have received from abroad for foodstuffs, I think some attention must be paid to this matter. The minister stated that approximately 177,000 men would be required for the armed forces during the coming year, and we all know that if our soldiers go into action soon, we shall have to supply reinforcements at a much greater rate than has been the situation to date. There is also the matter of our war production in Canada. We have been told by the government that something like $800,000,000 has been expended on plant and equipment in Canada, all of which must be manned. Then we have a large shipbuilding programme which requires a great many men, not only for the building of the ships but to man them after they are launched.
It seems to me that this man-power question in Canada has been perhaps the greatest muddle we have had to face. We had a man appointed last year to head the selective service who, I believe, would have solved this problem if he had been allowed to carry on. He was dismissed, however, although since his dismissal the government have had to adopt at least some of the measures he proposed, and I believe they will have to adopt more of them before this problem is finally solved. The government now propose, under selective service, to take many men out of non-essential industries and make them available where
2S74
Supply-Agriculture

labour is needed in essential industries. According to one statement, some two hundred thousand of these people will be transferred, and many of them will be placed in agriculture. The Minister of National Defence said there would be still available a considerable number of men who might undertake more active service if they could be replaced by women, and I would suggest that the government go farther in the matter of taking women out of non-essential industries. I hold in my hand a copy of The Rural Co-operator, published in Toronto by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. It commends the government for the stand they have taken in transferring men from non-essential industry, and goes on to say:
Another source of man-power and woman-power would be among those employed for personal service so that their employers can spend their time playing bridge or doing something equally unimportant to the national welfare. All the people we know who are doing big jobs do not seem to require staffs of private chauffeurs or parlour maids. But simply because certain people happened to have acquired much money the following ad appears in a Toronto paper, even in our fourth year of war.
"Parlour maid wanted for May 1, four in family, three maids kept. Apply employment and selective service, 832 Bay street."
It appears to me that if our selective service cannot find more to do than look for third maids for families of four, we have not solved our problem of man-power and womampower in this country, and I would suggest that the government look into this point.
With regard to these people it is proposed to transfer from non-essential industries to agriculture, the wages paid by agriculture during the past three years have increased very greatly. I have in my hand some statistics from the dominion bureau giving the wage scales by provinces from 1941 to 1943, and also giving the average for Canada as a whole. In 1941 the average wage paid for farm help per day, as at January 15, was $1.24 with board. In 1943 this had risen to $2.02. In August, 1941, the average wage paid farm help in Canada was $1.52; in 1942 it was $2.50, and I may add that there has been another increase in 1943. As a matter of fact; just before I boarded the train to return to Ottawa after the Easter recess I had a visit from a farmer who seemed to be rather peeved. He wanted to know what the blankety-blank we were doing here in Ottawa in regard to farm wages. I asked what was the trouble and he said, "Well, a month ago I hired a man to work on my farm for the summer at $75 a month. Last week, when I was ready to start seeding,
	. ,u
he told me he wanted $85. I agreed to give him $85 a month, but this morning he said he wanted $100. I told him to pack his bag, and I brought him to town with me. Now I do not know how I am going to get in my crop." That may not be general, but I know it has occurred in western Canada as a result of the scarcity of labour; and these increased wages are not the only additional costs the farmer has to meet.
If you transfer men from non-essential industries to the farms, many of these men will know nothing about farming but they will ask the same wages as those paid to experienced help. Any farmer knows that inexperienced help costs at least twice as much as experienced help, even though the wages may be the same. That was what we found last fall, when large harvest excursions were run to the west from eastern Canada. I would say that 50 per cent of those who went west on those excursions had no farm experience, yet they asked the same wages, $5 and $6 a day, as those that were being paid to experienced help.
If we are to get the necessary production in this country; if we are to supply the food1 being asked for by Great Britain., we shall have to do something about this labour situation. There is a food shortage in Canada, whether we are ready to admit it or not. In this evening's Ottawa Journal we find a1 statement that housewives are having to pay five cents apiece for potatoes. The article reads:
"I wouldn't be surprised if they were," commented L. F. Burrows, secretary of the Canadian fruit wholesalers' association, to-day when informed of reports that Ottawa housewives were paying up to five cents each for potatoes. [DOT] *
"There is an acute shortage of potatoes all over Canada and the United States," Mr. Burrows said. "Everything possible is being done by the prices board to ensure a fair distribution of what potatoes are available."
