speechtext: Did he say how heavy the potatoes were?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext:
No; but I imagine it
would have to be a large potato to be worth1 five cents. We have price, ceilings in Canada, and there is a ceiling on wages in every industry with the exception of agriculture. I suggest fhat the government should give serious consideration to setting minimum and maximum farm wages so that farmers may have some idea of what their labour will cost. We should be fair with the men who are to go from non-essential industries into agriculture. Many of these men have families which

Supply-A g riculture
will have to be maintained in the cities, and I doubt if they will be able to maintain them with the wages they will earn in agriculture.
The government should consider paying a subsidy to these men so that they will be able to keep their families and so that agriculture may have their services at prices the farmer is able to pay. Ceiling prices apply to many products, and if there is no ceiling on agricultural costs there will be a reduction in production. A farmer is only going to go through one experience of hiring inexperienced help, because with inexperienced help it is more trouble to produce than it is under ordinary circumstances. The result will be that he will cut his production. The government should give serious consideration to this matter of farm wages and the effect that any increase in wages will have upon the production of this country.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext:
I should like to support what the hon. member has said. I raised this question with the Minister of Finance during a debate this winter, and he said he could not give me any answer. I pointed out that in settling the steel strike last fall the government had, by order in council guaranteed the workers a base of fifty-five cents an hour, plus cost-of-living bonus. I went on to point out to the house, as the hon. member has done this evening, the wages that are being paid on farms this spring. In my opinion, farm help are entitled to the same consideration given to labour in industry and to steel workers. I placed on Hansard figures to show what it would cost a farmer for his help if he paid fifty-five cents an hour, plus a living bonus. It was considerably more than the $75 and $85 a month that is now being paid.
During the last session I had1 many discussions with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Labour, and I bring up .the matter again to-night because both these ministers are in their places. If we are to maintain the price ceiling, the government will have to face this problem. I trust that these ministers will bring pressure to bear on their colleagues in the government and have this matter taken care of. I am not urging that the farm worker should work for a lower wage than is paid to labour in industry, and therefore it will be necessary for the government to bonus farm labour or adopt some other means of solving this problem.. As has been pointed out, inefficient farm labour is very costly. I would rather pay a good man who I knew would take care of my power equipment twice what I might have to pay inexperienced help, because I know I would be farther ahead in the long run. I trust the government will be able to give us some assurance in this regard.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: I am not just clear what the hon. member is advocating. Is he advocating that there should be a ceiling on wages or that the government should pay a subsidy?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: I am not so sure just which should be done. When I spoke before, I advocated the payment of a bonus. If we are to maintain ceiling prices throughout this country, we must realize that farm labour is entitled to the same remuneration as is paid to labour in other industries.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: In the other industries the cost of living bonus is not paid by the government; it is paid by the employer.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: In many instances the government purchase the product, and in that way they are really paying the cost of living bonus. We have been given the details of the great cost of subsidizing these different productions in order to keep down the cost of living. I aim not so much concerned about how you bring this about, but you must either let agricultural prices rise or you must bonus labour in order that our farmer's can produce and receive some degree of parity.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: If there is no rise in the cost of living index, -there is no rise in the cost of living bonus.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: A moment ago the Minister of Agriculture said that the government did not pay the cost of living bonus, but as a matter of fact many of the war materials are produced on a cost-plus basis and the government does pay the cost of living bonus. While the manufacturer pays it in the first place, the government pays it when it buys the product.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRIVY COUNCIL OF QUESTION OF CANADIAN JURISDICTION
speechtext: The government does the same thing with farm products. We pay an advance on wheat and we take delivery of bacon and pay delivery costs at the port. The same is true of cheese and many other farm products.
